steps.title: Wrong column first
steps.caption: Only (created_at, customer_id) exists: customer 42's history walks 52,936 entries to find 20 rows.
steps.body: Acme Shop already has an index on **(created_at, customer_id)**. The history screen asks for customer 42's 20 newest delivered orders, and the best PostgreSQL 18 can do with that index is walk it backward from the newest entry, checking `customer_id = 42` on each one: 52,936 entries and 226 buffers for 20 rows. For customer 1012, with 34 orders, the planner gives up on the index: it reads all 5,058 table pages and sorts.

steps.title: Leftmost prefix
steps.caption: Swap the columns: customer_id = 42 becomes one slice of 179 entries, already sorted by created_at.
steps.body: A B-tree on (a, b) is sorted by `a`, and by `b` only among entries with the same `a`. On **(customer_id, created_at)** an equality on the leading column lands on one contiguous slice, customer 42's 179 entries, and inside it the entries are already in `created_at` order. A condition on `created_at` alone has no single range to seek to: its matches sit in every customer's slice.

steps.title: Equality first, sort last
steps.caption: History: seek to the slice end, read 20 entries, stop (23 buffers). Dashboard: (status, created_at).
steps.body: After `CREATE INDEX ON orders (customer_id, created_at)` the plan is again an Index Scan Backward with `Index Cond: (customer_id = 42)`, but now it seeks to the end of the slice, takes 20 entries newest first and stops: 23 buffers and no Sort node. The dashboard (`status = 'pending' AND created_at >= '2026-10-02'`) follows the same rule with **(status, created_at)**, equality first and range last, so it reads exactly its 210 entries: 213 buffers instead of 526.

steps.title: Skip scan and the costs
steps.caption: Skip scan: (status, created_at) serves created_at alone too. Every index is written on every insert.
steps.body: With PostgreSQL 18's **skip scan**, (status, created_at) also answers `created_at >= '2026-10-02'` with no status condition: 6 index searches over its 5 statuses, 579 buffers, so the old (created_at, customer_id) index can go if nothing else needs it. (customer_id, created_at) couldn't stand in: with 95,880 customers to skip, the planner would rather read the whole table. Every index is written on every INSERT (5 WAL records here with four indexes, 2 with the primary key alone), and an index on (customer_id) alone would be redundant next to (customer_id, created_at).
